newsitem.title: GERMANY: F.O.Licht - Second world sugar balance estimate.
newsitem.headline: F.O.Licht - Second world sugar balance estimate.

text.p: The following is a direct contribution from statistician F.O. Licht of Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.
SECOND ESTIMATE OF THE WORLD SUGAR BALANCE 1996/97 -

Despite several changes to individual figures, the overall production and consumption totals for the sugar year September/August 1996/97 show little change from our first forecasts published at the end of October, 1996. We have reduced our world production estimate by 0.6 per cent while consumption is up by 0.6 per cent. Production is still well in excess of indicated consumption which points to a rise in stocks of 2.1 million tonnes. The stock/consumption ratio, even though lower than forecast in October, remains above 40 percent, the highest figure since 1985/86 when, allowing for inflation, prices were at a similarly low level.

Weather conditions have favoured production in the EU this season and output is expected to be up by about 755,000 tonnes after roughly half a million tonnes last season. Output in Yugoslavia and Turkey is also expected to rise sharply with the latter country possibly becoming an exporter. In East Europe output in Poland reached 2.5 million tonnes but industries in the two important beet growing countries further to the East still struggle with the chaotic conditions. Much the same can be said for the industries in many other countries in East Europe.

Nothing strange is expected from Africa where output is expected to reach 8.6 million tonnes compared with 8.2 million tonnes last season. The big problem in North & Central America is what will be produced in Cuba. Hurricane Lili and the effect of the Helms-Burton law will between them scupper any chance of the target of 5.2/5.3 million tonnes being reached but it is difficult to forecast by how far output will fall short of its goal. Expanding beet sugar production has led to a somewhat higher output in the USA than had originally been forecasted while Mexico will match last season's 4.8 million tonnes. Output in South America has been growing rapidly, largely because of the burgeoning production in Brazil. It is possible that the current level of world prices will bring further expansion to a halt. Price considerations combined with current stocking problems will certainly lead to a drop in output in India. Thailand is expecting another good crop but price factors are likely to lead to lower expansion in future. Production growth could also slow in Australia if prices do not improve.

World consumption is now put at 120 million tonnes, up from 117 million tonnes the previous year. Not much change is expected in the EU but demand is expected to rise in both Yugoslavia and Turkey. In 1989/90 Russian consumption reached 7.5 million tonnes. Where it is now is difficult to estimate, but it is probably in the region of 5.0/5.5 million tonnes. Consumption has also dropped in the Ukraine and is now probably around 2.2 million tonnes. Because of the high level of production consumption is also likely to rise in Poland, while some unregistered cross border trade may also help to swell apparent domestic needs. Consumption in Africa is likely to rise slightly, mostly reflecting population growth. Offtake in North & Central America is continuing to rise, led by the USA with more than half the total. Brazil has similar dominant positions in South America where usage is expected to reach 8.6 million tonnes out of a total of 14.2 million tonnes. Consumption in Asia is expected to rise by 3.6 per cent reflecting high population growth and lower per capita consumption. After an increase of 6 per cent last year a further sharp increase is looked for in India, reflecting the abundant stocks. Consumption in China is expected to reach 8.6 million tonnes, up from 8.3 million tonnes last year, while in Pakistan it is likely to rise by more than 3 per cent. In Oceania growth is now expected to be slightly higher than forecast earlier.

Gross import demand is still forecast to fall by about 1.8 million tonnes from last year's 38.0 million tonnes. In Western Europe Yugoslavia and Turkey will import less than last year but higher imports by the USA will lead to an increase of more than 10 per cent in North & Central America. The big change will be in Asia where import demand is expected to fall from 15.2 to 13.7 million tonnes. The Philippines will be primarily responsible for this fall but Indonesia and China are also expected to reduce their imports.

Though still over 40 percent, our stock/consumption ratio is lower than previously estimated. But the change has occurred in India so that the lower surplus figure will have little impact on world market prices. The distinction between raw and white sugar is becoming cloudy with so much lower quality white sugar now coming onto the market.
